$meta.name: Robo Story-First Presentation Contract
$meta.description: Decision-first reasoning and QA rules that sit above semantic layouts and brand styling.
$meta.adaptation: Robo-specific synthesis. This contract is authoritative for Robo decks; the external source is inspiration, not a dependency.

workflow.label: Frame the decision
workflow.rule: Define the audience, decision or action, evidence boundary, and required output before slide design.

workflow.label: Write the governing claim
workflow.rule: State the deck conclusion first, then write one conclusion-oriented headline per slide before drawing.

workflow.label: Build the headline ledger
workflow.rule: For multi-slide decks, verify that headlines form a coherent argument and that peer slides use one consistent split.

workflow.label: Choose intent and archetype
workflow.rule: Select the slide's communication intent first, then select a numbered archetype, then map it to the closest supported semantic layout.

workflow.label: Apply semantic layout and brand grammar
workflow.rule: Use the semantic layout as the rendering contract and the selected Robo brand as the visual grammar.

workflow.label: Measure and verify
workflow.rule: Run structural QA, render the deck, and inspect overflow, collisions, hierarchy, consistency, and evidence traceability.

rules: One slide has one governing message.
Prefer a complete claim with an explicit judgment or implication over a topic label.
Keep evidence and judgment in the same headline when it remains readable.
Use sentence-pattern variety across adjacent slides.
Do not use the headline to count elements; use it to state what the elements mean.
Move secondary evidence into the body before weakening the claim.
antiPatterns: two disconnected claims joined only by punctuation
self-reference such as 'this slide' or 'this page'
ornamental slogans that cannot be proven by the body

rules: Headlines read alone should reconstruct the core argument.
Adjacent slides should have an explicit logical bridge such as cause, consequence, contrast, or evidence.
Sibling slides should share one segmentation logic and comparable granularity.
Decision decks should identify the questions that require an explicit choice.
The final decision slide should resolve decisions, owners or timing rather than merely summarize.
Every material number needs a source, a stated calculation basis, or an explicit placeholder.
Facts, assumptions, estimates, recommendations, and decisions must remain distinguishable.
Each major clause in a headline should be supported by a visible body element.
Do not fabricate screenshots, quotes, system output, customer names, or measured results.

lineStyles.dashed: forecast, plan, alternative, or disappearing state
lineStyles.dotted: supporting boundary, reference, or secondary relation

rules: Choose axes before placing objects.
Do not introduce a third visual axis into one diagram; split the view instead.
Encode magnitude with proportional length, area, width, or weight when magnitude is part of the claim.
Keep compared elements in stable positions whenever possible.
Use color semantically and sparingly; brand variants remain the source of truth for actual colors.

headline: claim is complete and decision-relevant
body visibly supports the headline
no topic-only or self-referential title
no unsupported numeric precision
story: headlines form a coherent vertical argument
peer slides use one split and consistent granularity
decision questions are introduced and resolved
visual: no orphaned one- or two-character line breaks
line and fill semantics stay consistent
comparison axes and positions are comparable
whitespace is intentional rather than leftover

exceptions: These are defaults, not immutable laws. A deviation is acceptable when it improves truthfulness, accessibility, or decision clarity.
The semantic layout contract and brand contract remain authoritative for what the current renderer can generate.
